messages.subject: Small area estimation
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am trying to fit a spatial-temporal model using small area estimation for malnutrition data.

A brief description of my data.

My data is at child level (binary data), clustered at different clusters within counties and spans for period of 7 years. Some of the clusters within which child level data is collected are georeferenced while some are not.

I need to fit a spatial-temporal model that can take into account the child level data, both the georeferenced data and the one that is not georeferenced, but make predictions at county level.

I tried a number of approaches by fitting this two models shown below.

### add some NA's to the year I want to predict

mal.data.stunt $y[mal.data.stunt $year==2] <- NA

# formula

Model1= y ~  1 + f(County.ID, model="besag", graph="mapkenya.graph",

                           group=Year.ID, control.group=list(model="ar1",

                                                       hyper=list(theta=list(param=c(0,1)))))

And;

Model2=y ~ 1 + f(Year.ID2, model='ar1') +

                f(County.ID2, model="besag", graph="mapkenya.graph") +

                f(County.ID, model="besag", graph="mapkenya.graph",

                  group=Year.ID, control.group=list(model="ar1",

                                              hyper=list(theta=list(param=c(0,1))))))

Inla.model.1<-inla(Model1,

             family="binomial",

             data=mal.data.stunt,

             Ntrials=dim(mal.data.stunt)[1],

             control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,cpo=T),

             verbose=T

)

Model 1;

Models the interaction of space and time.

Model 2;

Models the spatial effect, temporal effect and the interaction of space and time.

I have several questions;

1.       If I want to do predictions, (say year 2) at county level, how do I specify in my model, because when I run either one of the models above, I have predictions at child level instead of county level?

2.       Should I change my data from binary to count and compute the ratio between the numbers of observed cases of malnourishment (say stunting) and the number of expected cases in every county using census population counts?

Sorry for the length of my question.

Thanks.

Thomas

Hi,

good question. I understand well that this is confusing

the inla-output in the result object is not clear on this point, which
is a consequence of the output not being 'designed' for suchs. the
holde'output' should be redesigned at some point...

anyway, here is how

if the model X is replicated Y times, then the output is

c(X.rep1, X.rep2, ..., X.repY)

I added a small test which demonstrate this

the issue gets more involved if the model is also 'grouped' by
introducing some dependence and then replicated. then the storage is

X.group1.rep1, X.group2.rep1, ...., X.groupG.rep1, X.group1.rep2, ....

the function

	inla.idx

defines this, and can compute the index where each element is found.
like

> inla.idx(3, n=10,replicate=3, nrep=3, group=1,ngroup=1)
[1] 23

so with three replicates and no group (ie ngroup=1), then the index for
x[3] at replicate 3,  is 23.

hope this helps,
H

messages.body_plain:
Dear inla-group,
When using SPDE models, default priors may result in overparametrized models (high number of effective parameters, low number of equivalent replicates).
I wonder how to define 'better' priors alleviating this undesirable effect. I expect this can be achieved by changing parameters within the inla.spde2.matern() function.
Without apriori knowledge, I expect that range (prior.range.nominal) and variance (prior.variance.nominal) parameters (or alternatively tau and kappa mean parameters) should be let to default ones.
It remains the precision parameter of thetas (theta.prior.prec). Is testing different values for this parameter and looking at posterior results (e.g. number of effective parameters and cpo) a good solution to identify 'better' priors?
If so, Is precision for tau and kappa should be the same for estimate a stationnary field?
Best regards,
Kévin

> Dear inla-group,
> When using SPDE models, default priors may result in overparametrized models (high number of effective parameters, low number of equivalent replicates).

Hi Kévin,

Ingebrigtsen, et al. (http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211675313000377 and http://arxiv.org/pdf/1412.2798v2.pdf) discusses some of the issues you bring up: mean and variance for Gaussian prior for the stationary part and how to select the variances for the priors on the non-stationarity parameters.

However, recently, there has been a recent drive towards developing new priors based on "Penalised Complexity" (http://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.4630v4.pdf) in the INLA group and this is currently being extended also to spatial and non-stationary spatial models (http://arxiv.org/pdf/1503.00256v1.pdf). The prior for the stationary model can be specified without too much hassle, but the documentation for doing that is currently lacking, and the prior for the non-stationary model is work-in-progress and does not have an easy interface. If you are interested in exploring this avenue, you can contact me.

As for the second part on evaluating the different priors, I think it will depend on the goal of the analysis. If the choice of prior leads to better cpo scores, the predictive distributions are better and one could argue that if predictions are the main goal, the prior is 'better'. But if the goal is to decide whether non-stationarity is present or whether a certain covariate is affecting non-stationarity, I'm not sure if it would be appropriate to base the selection of the prior on the predictive properties of the model. First of all, it is not completely Bayesian and, secondly, using the data twice might lead to biases.

--
Geir-Arne

Geir-Arne's comments are good.
Further to that, there are some simple things that can be done better than the defaults.
The default prior range is usually ok, but the default prior for the variance can easily be completely inappropriate, as it depends on the scale of the latent component (and not necessarily the scale of the data itself).  The minimum approach that can take that into account is included here:
  http://www.r-inla.org/examples/tutorials/spde-tutorial-from-jss
For example, the prior median "sigma0" in the examples should be set to something more sensible than the default, 1.

In retrospect, I wish I had let the code give an error (or at least a warning) if the user doesn't specify any prior distribution parameters, as that isn't very Bayesian!
When the newer approaches are mature enough to use on all spde models, we may consider not allowing any preset "default" priors at all.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Alpha=1 is a CAR(1), and alpha=2 is a CAR(2).

In 1d, the continuous limits have smoothness 0.5 and 1.5, respectively; alpha=1 corresponds to a discretised ornstein-uhlenbeck process.

In 2d, the alpha=1 case does not have a _pointwise_ limit, since the smoothness is 0. The limit is only defined with respect to integrals over subregions (hence the "with care"; you  need to consider which integrals your discretised model corresponds to). See papers by Besag and Mondal&Besag for details (references are in the 2011 Lindgren et al paper on the precise connection between GMRfs and SPDEs and Matérn models)
Alpha=2 on the other hand gives smoothness 1, so the continuous limit is well-behaved.

If only point estimates are desired, one does not always see a big difference, especially if regular lattices are used. The differences however are very important for posterior uncertainties, and in particular when irregular meshes are used.

If there is lots of data so that it dominates the prior, then the model doesn't matter so much.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Dear Forum,

I am trying to implement a Distributed Lag Model (see ref bellow) in INLA.

Gasparrini, A. (2014), Modeling exposure–lag–response associations with
distributed lag non-linear models. Statist. Med., 33: 881–899.

That is something like : for t = 1,...,n,

y_t = sum_{ k in 0 to lag} w(k)*x_{t-k} + eps_t  (1)

where w(k) is a smooth function along k.
To this end, I used the A-matrix feature in INLA:

y ~ A %*% eta
eta ~ f(w,x,model="rw2")

where A is defined according to model (1) and
y=(y_{t},y_{t-1},....)
w=rep(1:lag,n) and
x=(x_{t},....,x_{t-lag},x_{t-1},...,x_{t-1-lag},....)

The model seems to work well but the predicted curve overfit
the data (see the generated plot in the following example).
Any advice?

# simple example in INLA
rm(list=ls())
require(scales)
require(INLA)
set.seed(1234)
lag=5
n=100
x=sin(1:n/10)/(1:n/10)
y=x*NA
for(t in lag:n) y[t]=x[t]+.5*x[t-2]-2*x[t-4] + rnorm(1,sd=.01)

y0=y;y[50:80]<-NA #To check model prediction

####### Augmented model with the
index=kronecker(1:n,1:lag,FUN = "+")-lag
index[index<=0]=NA
X <- x[index]
i  <- rep(1:lag,n)        # indices for w_l
A=kronecker(diag(n),t(rep(1,lag))) #
# formulating the model with the A-matrix feature
formula <- Y ~ -1 + f(i,X,model="iid",constr=FALSE)
fit <- inla(formula, data = list(Y=y,X=X,i=i),
    control.compute=list(dic=TRUE),
    control.predictor=list(A=A,compute=TRUE)
    )
plot(y[lag:n],type="l",lwd=3,ylab="y",ylim=range(y,na.rm=TRUE)*1.2)
lines(y0[lag:n],col=alpha("grey30",.2),lwd=5)
lines(fit$summary.fitted.values$mean[lag:n],col=alpha("blue",.2),lwd=5)

Yes, you can use inla.stack() to build models of the type

Predictor(i) = \sum_k \sum_j A_k(i,j) h_k(effect_k)(j)

In matrix form, that's
Eta^* = sum_k A_k h_k(effect_k)

h_k is the model result for effect k (e.g. Linear, rw2 function, bym, ...)

In you example, if eta was just a fixed effect, you'd have two A matrices:
A * eta  + Identity * h(region)

The inla.stack() parameters for that would look like this:
A = list(A, Diagonal(length(region))
effects = list(list(eta=eta), list(region=region))

Finn

Hi Alex,

You have a set of of disconnected regions and want a model such that the
process into each region is treated as  replicas. The easier way to do
it is to  build a mesh that has nodes only inside each of these regions.
You can include outer extension by adding a buffer into each region
before running the following commands.

require(rgdal)
map <- readOGR('./', 'SA_LB_PCsimple_L93')

require(INLA)
bound <- inla.sp2segment(map)
(el <- mean(apply(bbox(map), 1, function(x) 0.03*diff(x))))
(mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary=bound, max.edge=el))$n

plot(map)
plot(mesh, add=TRUE)

Elias

messages.subject_clean: Reconstructing confidence intervals for interaction terms
messages.body_plain:
This is, I hope, a very quick question – certainly a basic one! I've been building some models using inla that have an interaction term included between two variables. This is often very important in my data. I get a nice summary of my model using summary(mod1) that includes the confidence intervals. In the data I have, when the value of the interacting factor is false there is often an obviously significant positive effect of by dependent variable, but the raw data suggest that the slope for data when the factor is TRUE is pretty close to zero. This is exactly what we predicted, so I'm quite excited, but I'm trying to work out the correct way to recover credible intervals for the slopes in both cases.

EG summary results:

variable                   mean    sd   0.025     0.5   0.0975   kld

(Intercept):                   2.3   0.3     0.1      2.2       4.1     0

rain:                            10.1  2.3      6.3    10.1    17.5     0

FactorTRUE:               0.2  0.01   0.05     0.21    0.32    0

rain:FactorTRUE:     -10.3    3.2   -5.3   -10.2    -19.4    0

Since FALSE is the reference level, I think the slope and its intervals are simply described by the output table. (e.g. median = 10.1 low = 6.3, upper = 17.5)

I also think the median value for the slope in the TRUE case is close enough to the sum of the median for the reference level and the interaction term (-0.1: essentially zero). But the credible intervals for the interaction are not the sum of the lower and upper intervals (i.e. not 6.3-5.3 and 17.5-19.4), since the chance of getting the lowest likely parameter value for both factor levels in the same model are obviously much lower than they should be (0.025^2). I'm sure calculating this joint interval so I can correctly extract the credible intervals (for plotting or whatever – in this case showing that is correctly overlaps zero) is easy – but not from the summary table and I can't work out how to correctly calculate this from the inla object.
